why_how.text: Legal medicines as well as illegal drugs can weaken driving, so ask your doctor about side effects and know the risks.
Mixing alcohol with drugs multiplies the danger and has cost lives.

scenario.text: Sam has a cold and takes an over-the-counter cold pill before a long drive.

reasoning.text: Some cold pills contain antihistamines, which can cause inattention, confusion and drowsiness.

result.text: Sam checks the ingredients and does not drive while drowsy, and never adds alcohol to the medicine.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a drink with a pill only doubles the effect.

correction.text: Combining alcohol with drugs multiplies the effect rather than doubling it, and it has caused deaths.

memory_support.text: Read the label, ask the doctor, skip the drink.

prompt.text: What should you ask your doctor when you start a prescription medicine?

answer.text: About any side effects that could affect your driving.

rationale.text: Prescription medicines can weaken driving, so the manual says to ask the doctor about side effects related to driving.

lines.text: Prescribed or over the counter.
Illegal drugs and the alcohol mix.

narration.text: Alcohol is not the only substance that can make driving dangerous. Many drugs can weaken your ability to drive safely, whether a doctor prescribed them or you bought them over the counter. In this lesson you will learn what to ask your doctor, which ingredients in common cold and allergy pills can affect driving, what antihistamines and barbiturates do, why illegal drugs and marijuana have no place behind the wheel, why mixing alcohol and drugs is especially deadly, and who is responsible for telling a person with a chronic illness about driving limits.

lines.text: Ask your doctor about side effects.
Cold pills may hold codeine or alcohol.

narration.text: When you take prescription medicine, ask your doctor about any side effects that could affect your driving. Over-the-counter remedies need care too. Some non-prescription allergy remedies and cold pills contain codeine, alcohol, antihistamines or bromides, and each of these can affect driving. Antihistamines, taken for cold congestion and allergies, can cause inattention, confusion and drowsiness, and some are even used as sleep aids. So read labels, and if a medicine makes you drowsy or confused, do not drive until it has worn off. When in doubt about a medicine, do not drive.

lines.text: Barbiturates: drunk-like when overused.
LSD, heroin, marijuana: do not drive.

narration.text: Barbiturates are sedatives used mainly for sleep, and overusing them brings drowsiness, confusion and poor coordination much like drunkenness, leaving the person unfit to drive. The most dangerous drugs, such as LSD and heroin, are available only illegally and can leave users unaware of their surroundings, so no one under their influence may drive. Studies cited in the manual link marijuana use to more traffic-violation arrests, and experts agree it should not be used when driving. Each of these can take away the alertness that safe driving depends on.

lines.text: Alcohol plus drugs multiplies the effect.
Never drink while taking medicine.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some people believe that if a pill gives one effect, a drink with it just doubles it. The manual says that is wrong. Combining alcohol with drugs does not merely double the effect; it multiplies it, and the combination has caused deaths. That is why you should never drink while taking medicine. Remember too that some cold pills already contain alcohol. And keep the two drug effects straight: antihistamines may cause drowsiness and confusion as side effects, while barbiturates produce drunk-like symptoms when used to excess.

lines.text: Starting a prescription: what to ask?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: what should you ask your doctor when you start a prescription medicine? Decide first, then listen. The answer is to ask about any side effects that could affect your driving. Many drugs, prescribed or bought over the counter, can weaken your ability to drive safely, and your doctor can tell you what to watch for. For a chronic illness or physical impairment, the physician also has the responsibility to tell you about any driving limits that may apply, so that conversation protects you and everyone else on the road. When in doubt about a medicine, do not drive.

lines.text: Ask, read labels, never mix with alcohol.
Doctors explain driving limits.

narration.text: To sum up, many drugs, prescribed or over the counter, can weaken safe driving, so ask your doctor about driving side effects. Some cold and allergy pills contain codeine, alcohol, antihistamines or bromides, and antihistamines can cause inattention, confusion and drowsiness. Overused barbiturates bring drunk-like symptoms. No one under the influence of drugs like LSD or heroin may drive, and experts agree marijuana should not be used when driving. Alcohol with drugs multiplies the effect and has caused deaths, and for chronic illness the physician explains any driving limits.

why_how.text: Following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, and the gap ahead is the space you control best.

scenario.text: Pat is driving in heavy rain on the highway behind a pickup.

reasoning.text: Two seconds is for good conditions; in poor weather the manual says to stretch the gap to four or five seconds.

result.text: Pat picks a sign post, counts as the pickup passes it, and eases off until four or five seconds pass before reaching it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking two seconds is enough in every kind of weather.

correction.text: Two seconds is the count for good conditions; poor roads, bad weather or a long vehicle call for four or five seconds.

memory_support.text: Two in good weather, four or five in bad.

prompt.text: How do you use a fixed object to check your following distance?

answer.text: Start counting one thousand one, one thousand two as the car ahead passes it, and ease off if you reach it first.

rationale.text: If you reach the object before finishing the count, you are too close and should slow until the gap is safe.

lines.text: Most rear-end crashes: following too close.
Control the space ahead.

narration.text: This lesson is about the space between your car and the vehicle ahead. Following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, and the space ahead of your car, called following distance, is the space you can control most easily. You will learn how to set your following distance, why the old car-length rule gave way to the two-second rule, exactly how to count two seconds, when to stretch the gap to four or five seconds, and what to do with your foot when you see brake lights ahead. These are habits that prevent some of the most common crashes.

lines.text: Match it to traffic speed and road.
Leave room to stop if you must.

narration.text: Set your following distance by the speed of traffic and the condition of the road, leaving enough room to stop if you must. The faster the traffic and the worse the road, the more room you need. For years drivers used a rule of thumb of one car length for every ten miles per hour. That old rule has given way to the two-second rule, which the manual calls easier to apply and safer. Counting time instead of guessing car lengths works at any speed, because the gap in feet grows automatically as you go faster. More space ahead means more time to react.

lines.text: Pick a fixed object ahead.
Count one thousand one, one thousand two.

narration.text: To use the two-second rule, pick a fixed object on the road ahead, such as a sign post, a tree or an overpass. When the vehicle ahead passes that object, start counting one thousand one, one thousand two. If you reach the object before you finish the count, you are following too closely, and you should ease off until the gap is safe. Check again after you slow down. This simple count works on any road and at any speed, which is why it replaced the old car-length method. Practice it until it becomes a habit you use without thinking. More space ahead means more time to react.

lines.text: Poor road or weather: four or five seconds.
Long vehicles need the longer gap too.

narration.text: Two seconds is the count for good conditions. When road or weather conditions are poor, stretch the gap to a four- or five-second count. Use the longer gap too when you are driving a vehicle that is longer than a car. Rain, a slick road surface or a long vehicle all mean you need more distance to stop, so the count goes up. Treat the two seconds as the minimum, not the target. Whenever conditions are less than ideal, leave the longer gap and the extra space that comes with it. More space ahead means more time to react. The gap ahead is the space you control best.

lines.text: Good conditions: two seconds.
Bad conditions or long vehicles: four or five.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners memorize the two-second rule and apply it everywhere. But two seconds is only the count for good conditions. Bad roads, bad weather or a long vehicle call for four or five seconds. So when a question describes rain, ice, fog or a long vehicle and asks for the following count, two seconds is the wrong answer. The longer count gives you the extra stopping room those conditions demand. Read the conditions in the question first, then choose two seconds or four to five seconds to match. More space ahead means more time to react.

lines.text: How do you use a fixed object?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how do you use a fixed object to check your following distance? Settle on your answer first. The answer is to pick a fixed object ahead, start counting one thousand one, one thousand two as the vehicle ahead passes it, and ease off if you reach the object before you finish the count. Reaching it early means you are too close. Remember that this two-second count is for good conditions; in poor road or weather conditions, or in a long vehicle, stretch it to four or five seconds. More space ahead means more time to react.

lines.text: Two seconds, more when it is bad.
Watch brake lights; cover the brake.

narration.text: To wrap up, following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, and the space ahead is yours to control. Set the gap by traffic speed and road condition, using the two-second rule instead of car lengths: count from a fixed object and ease off if you arrive too soon. Stretch it to four or five seconds in poor conditions or a longer vehicle. And watch for brake lights and a shrinking gap ahead; when you see them, move your foot to the brake pedal right away so you are ready to stop if you need to. More space ahead means more time to react.

why_how.text: Knowing what lengthens stopping distance helps you choose a safe speed.
The chart shows how far a car travels before stopping, such as two hundred twenty-eight feet at fifty-five miles per hour.

scenario.text: Kim drives at sixty-five miles per hour and suddenly sees a hazard ahead.

reasoning.text: The chart shows seventy-one feet of thinking distance and two hundred thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance at that speed.

result.text: Kim needs a total of three hundred five point seven feet to stop, far more than at lower speeds.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking stopping distance is only about how hard you press the brake.

correction.text: Stopping distance depends first on reaction time and also on pavement, tires, brakes, the car's design and wind.

memory_support.text: Think, then brake; speed grows the brake part fastest.

prompt.text: According to the chart, what is the total stopping distance at fifty-five miles per hour?

rationale.text: At fifty-five the chart shows sixty feet while reacting and one hundred sixty-eight feet while braking.

lines.text: Many factors change stopping distance.
The chart shows thinking and braking.

narration.text: How far your car needs to stop helps decide what speed is safe. Stopping distance is not one fixed number; it depends on many factors. In this lesson you will learn the first and most important one, the driver's reaction time, and then the others: the pavement, the tires, the design and brakes of the car, and even the wind. Finally, you will read the manual's stopping-distance chart, which splits each stop into thinking distance and braking distance and shows how both grow as speed rises. The numbers may surprise you. Higher speed always means a longer stop.

lines.text: Reaction time comes first.
Rough dry concrete grips best.

narration.text: Actual stopping distance depends first on the driver's mental and physical reaction time, the moment between seeing a hazard and pressing the brake. Then the road matters. Pavement type and condition change stopping distance a great deal, since rough dry concrete grips far better than slippery brick or smooth asphalt. The same car and driver can need much more room to stop on a slick surface. So a safe speed is not just the posted limit; it depends on how quickly you can react and how well the surface lets your tires grip. Higher speed always means a longer stop.

lines.text: Type, condition and tread set traction.
Wide tires slip more when wet.

narration.text: Tire type, condition and tread depth all determine how much traction you have for stopping, so check the owner's manual or a dealer for the right tire size. Tire width matters too. Large, wide tires may stop sooner on smooth dry roads but skid or hydroplane more easily when wet, while small, narrow tires may cut through standing water yet lose overall stopping power. There is no perfect tire for every surface, which is why the right size for your car, in good condition with enough tread, is the safest choice. Higher speed always means a longer stop.

lines.text: Chassis, suspension, brakes and balance.
Tail wind affects sudden stops.

narration.text: The car's own design affects stopping. Chassis design, weight distribution, suspension, shock absorbers, and the type, condition and balance of the brakes all play a part. In an emergency, a brake that locks before the others can cause serious trouble, because the car may pull or skid. Conditions outside the car matter too. Wind direction and speed affect stopping, and drivers often do not realize how much difference a strong tail wind makes during a sudden high-speed stop. So keeping your brakes in balance and accounting for a strong tail wind both help.

lines.text: Twenty-five: sixty-one point seven feet total.
Fifty-five: two hundred twenty-eight feet total.

narration.text: The manual's stopping-distance chart splits each stop into thinking distance, covered while the driver reacts, and braking distance, covered after the brakes take hold. At twenty-five miles per hour, the chart gives twenty-seven feet of thinking distance plus thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance, sixty-one point seven feet in total. At fifty-five miles per hour, a driver covers sixty feet while reacting and one hundred sixty-eight feet while braking, two hundred twenty-eight feet in all. Notice how much longer the stop becomes.

lines.text: Sixty-five: seventy-one plus two thirty-four point seven.
Total: three hundred five point seven feet.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People expect stopping distance to grow evenly with speed, but the braking part grows much faster than the thinking part. At sixty-five miles per hour the chart shows seventy-one feet of thinking distance and two hundred thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance, a total of three hundred five point seven feet. Compare that with sixty-one point seven feet at twenty-five miles per hour. Thinking distance did not even triple, but braking distance grew to almost seven times as much. Higher speed costs far more stopping room.

lines.text: Total stopping distance at fifty-five?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: according to the chart, what is the total stopping distance at fifty-five miles per hour? Decide on your answer first. The answer is two hundred twenty-eight feet: sixty feet covered while reacting and one hundred sixty-eight feet while braking. At twenty-five miles per hour the total is only sixty-one point seven feet, and at sixty-five it is three hundred five point seven feet. Remember that the chart is a guide, and actual stopping distance also depends on reaction time, pavement, tires, brakes and wind. Higher speed always means a longer stop.

lines.text: Reaction, pavement, tires, brakes, wind.
Braking distance grows fastest with speed.

narration.text: To sum up, how far your car needs to stop helps decide a safe speed, and actual stopping distance depends first on reaction time. Rough dry concrete grips far better than slippery brick or smooth asphalt. Tire type, condition and tread set your traction; wide tires stop sooner on dry roads but slip more when wet, and narrow tires cut through water but lose stopping power. Chassis, suspension and brake balance matter, a brake that locks first can cause serious trouble, and a strong tail wind makes an unexpected difference in a sudden high-speed stop. The chart shows totals of sixty-one point seven, two hundred twenty-eight and three hundred five point seven feet.

why_how.text: The law requires you to stop and help after any crash, and knowing the steps keeps you and others safer.

scenario.text: Lee backs into a parked car in a lot and no one is around.

reasoning.text: After hitting an unattended vehicle, the manual says to notify police, try to find the owner, or leave a written note with your name and address.

result.text: Lee leaves a clearly visible note with name and address on the parked car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should always move injured people out of the car right away.

correction.text: Do not move injured people unless it is absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger.

prompt.text: After a crash, when may you move an injured person?

answer.text: Only when absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger.

rationale.text: Otherwise keep the injured lying or sitting down until trained medical help arrives.

lines.text: Stop, help and warn.
Share and collect information.

narration.text: No one plans to be in a crash, but every driver needs to know what to do if it happens. In this lesson you will learn your first duties at the scene: stopping, helping anyone who is injured, calling for medical help, and warning other traffic. Then you will see the limits on moving injured people and giving first aid, the information you must give and collect, what to do about insurance details, and how to handle hitting a vehicle with no one in it or damaging someone else's property. These duties apply in any type of crash. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: Stop at once; help the injured.
Warn traffic with flags or flares.

narration.text: If you are in a crash, you must stop at once and help anyone who is injured. Call for medical help if it is needed. Before the police arrive, warn other traffic with flags, flares or whatever you have, so that no one else drives into the scene. In any type of crash you must stop, tell the others involved your name, address and registration number, and let them see your driver license. These duties apply whether the crash is minor or serious, so stopping is never optional when you are involved. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: Move them only to escape danger.
Treat for shock, not too much aid.

narration.text: Moving injured people can make their injuries worse. Do not move them unless it is absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger, and keep them lying or sitting down until trained medical help arrives. Give first aid, keep the injured comfortable and treat for shock, but remember that a layman can give too much first aid. The manual recommends a Red Cross or similar first aid course, which can help you save a life and make you more safety-conscious. Knowing what not to do matters as much as knowing what to do. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: Not by default.
Only away from fire or danger.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people's instinct is to pull injured people out of a car right away. The manual says the opposite. Do not move injured people unless it is absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger, such as the threats common at a crash scene. Otherwise keep them lying or sitting down until trained medical help arrives. So when a question asks whether to move an injured person, look for the danger. With no fire or other danger, the right answer is to leave them still and give care where they are. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: Collect names, addresses and witnesses.
Share insurance details if asked.

narration.text: At a crash, collect the names and addresses of everyone involved and of any witnesses, and note other relevant details. If another person involved asks, give the name and address of your liability insurance company and your local agent. If you cannot provide that at the scene, provide it later. Together with your own name, address, registration number and license, this exchange lets everyone involved follow up properly. Keep a pen and paper in the car so you can record what you need, even when you are shaken. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: Police, owner, or a written note.
Tell any property owner.

narration.text: If you hit an unattended vehicle, you have three choices: notify the police, try to find its owner, or leave a written note with your name and address where it will easily be seen on that vehicle. Driving away without doing one of these is not an option. When a mishap damages any other kind of property, such as a fence or a mailbox, you must let the property owner know. The idea is the same in each case: the person whose vehicle or property you damaged must be able to reach you, even if they were not there. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: When may you move an injured person?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: after a crash, when may you move an injured person? Think about it before you hear the answer. The answer is only when it is absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger. Otherwise keep them lying or sitting down until trained medical help arrives, give first aid, keep them comfortable and treat for shock. And remember that a layman can give too much first aid. Your other first duties are to stop, help, call for medical help if needed and warn other traffic. Stopping is never optional when you are involved in a crash.

lines.text: Stop, help, warn, exchange.
Note on unattended cars; tell owners.

narration.text: To close, if you are in a crash, stop at once, help anyone injured, call for medical help if needed, and warn other traffic with flags or flares. Move injured people only when fire or another danger makes it absolutely necessary, keep them lying or sitting, treat for shock, and avoid giving too much first aid. Tell the others involved your name, address and registration number, let them see your license, collect names and addresses of those involved and witnesses, and give your insurer and agent if asked, even later. For an unattended vehicle, notify police, find the owner or leave a note, and tell any property owner about damage.

why_how.text: Reporting crashes quickly brings help, and the written form protects people when an at-fault driver has no insurance.

scenario.text: Dana is in a crash with five hundred dollars of damage, and the at-fault driver has no insurance.

reasoning.text: After a crash with five hundred dollars or more in damage, the involved driver has thirty days to send a written Form SR-thirty-one if the at-fault party was uninsured.

result.text: Dana sends the form to the ALEA Safety Responsibility Unit by mail or online within thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the written SR form replaces calling the police.

correction.text: An injury or fatal crash is reported to police right away; the written form within thirty days is a separate duty when an uninsured at-fault party is involved.

prompt.text: A crash injures someone on a state highway. Who must be told, and how fast?

answer.text: The State Troopers, by the fastest means available.

rationale.text: Injury or fatal crashes go to local police inside a city or town, or to the State Troopers on a state highway, by the fastest means.

lines.text: Report injury crashes right away.
The written SR form.

narration.text: After a crash, reporting is a legal duty, and it comes in two forms. First, a crash with injury or death must be reported right away to the right law enforcement agency. Second, in certain crashes a written form, Form SR-thirty-one, must be sent within thirty days. In this lesson you will learn which agency to call, when the form is required and when it is not, where it goes, and what a witness should include when reporting a crash. Keeping these two duties apart is the key to answering questions about them. Keep the two duties separate in your mind.

lines.text: Fastest means available.
City police or State Troopers.

narration.text: A crash with injury or death must be reported by the fastest means available. If it happens inside a city or town, report it to the local police. If it happens on a state highway, report it to the State Troopers. Speed matters because it brings medical help and officers to the scene quickly. If you witness a crash, give the exact location, say whether the road is blocked, and describe the likely damage and injuries. Every crash should be reported to the law enforcement agency that has jurisdiction over that road. Keep the two duties separate in your mind.

lines.text: Injury, death or five hundred dollars damage.
Due within thirty days if uninsured at fault.

narration.text: After a crash with injury, death or five hundred dollars or more in damage, the involved driver has thirty days to send a written Form SR-thirty-one if the at-fault party was uninsured. When both parties were insured, neither has to file it. The form goes to the ALEA Safety Responsibility Unit, either by mail or online through ALEA's driver license website. So the form depends on two things: the size of the crash, and whether the driver at fault had insurance. If both drivers were insured, there is no form to send. Keep the two duties separate in your mind.

lines.text: Police: right away.
SR form: within thirty days, if uninsured.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think the written form is how you report a crash, or that calling the police covers everything. They are separate duties. An injury or fatal crash is reported to police right away, by the fastest means. The written SR-thirty-one within thirty days applies when an uninsured at-fault party is involved, and it goes to the ALEA Safety Responsibility Unit. So a single crash can call for both: an immediate call to police and, later, a written form. Neither one replaces the other. Keep the two duties separate in your mind.

lines.text: Injury crash on a state highway?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a crash injures someone on a state highway. Who must be told, and how fast? Make your choice first. The answer is the State Troopers, by the fastest means available. Inside a city or town, the call would go to the local police instead. Separately, if the crash caused injury, death or five hundred dollars or more in damage and the at-fault driver was uninsured, the involved driver has thirty days to send the written SR-thirty-one form to ALEA by mail or online. Keep the two duties separate in your mind. Quick reports bring help sooner.

lines.text: Fast call to the right agency.
SR form within thirty days when required.

narration.text: To close, report any crash with injury or death by the fastest means, to local police in a city or town or to the State Troopers on a state highway. Witnesses should give the exact location, whether the road is blocked, and the likely damage and injuries. After a crash with injury, death or five hundred dollars or more in damage, the involved driver has thirty days to send Form SR-thirty-one if the at-fault party was uninsured, and neither files it when both were insured. The form goes to ALEA by mail or online. Keep the two duties separate in your mind.

why_how.text: Trains cannot stop quickly, so reading crossing warnings correctly can save your life.
Some vehicles must always stop at crossings, and drivers behind them must be ready.

scenario.text: Chris approaches a crossing as the red lights begin to flash and the gates start to come down.

reasoning.text: Flashing lights always mean stop, and with gates you stay stopped until they rise and the lights quit flashing.

result.text: Chris stops within fifteen to fifty feet of the crossing and waits until the gates rise and the lights stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the round yellow railroad sign marks the crossing itself.

correction.text: The round sign stands seven hundred fifty feet before the track as an advance warning; the crossbuck stands at the crossing.

memory_support.text: Round sign warns, crossbuck marks, lights and gates stop.

prompt.text: Which vehicles must stop before every railroad crossing?

answer.text: School buses, church buses, all passenger buses, and trucks hauling flammables, explosives or other hazardous material.

rationale.text: These vehicles always stop, while other drivers stop for flashing lights, lowered gates or an approaching train.

lines.text: Signs, markings, lights and gates.
Who must stop, and where.

narration.text: Railroad crossings use a set of warnings that build as you get closer, and each one tells you something different. In this lesson you will learn the round yellow advance sign, the markings painted on the pavement, flashing lights and gates, what to do at a crossing with no warning device, and the crossbuck sign at the crossing itself. Then you will see which vehicles must stop at every crossing, where a stop must be made, how to approach, and the rules for lowered gates and crossings with more than one track. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Round yellow sign, seven hundred fifty feet.
X, RR, no-passing and stop lines.

narration.text: The round railroad warning sign is yellow with a black X and the letters RR, and it stands seven hundred fifty feet before the track to warn of a crossing ahead. Before a crossing the pavement may also carry a large X with two R's. A yellow line painted ahead of the crossing means no passing, and white lines beside the track mark where to stop when a train is coming. Together these give you plenty of warning, so you can slow down early rather than discovering the crossing at the last moment. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Flashing lights: always stop.
Gates: stay stopped until they rise.

narration.text: When crossing lights start flashing, you must always stop and wait until it is safe to go. Red flashing lights also warn you to stop as crossing gates come down, and you stay stopped until the gates rise and the lights quit flashing. At a crossing with no warning device, slow down and look and listen for trains before going on. The crossbuck sign appears at most crossings and means slow down and be ready to stop when a train is seen; a sign under it shows the number of tracks when there is more than one. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Round sign: seven hundred fifty feet ahead.
Crossbuck: at the crossing.

narration.text: Here is a trap with railroad signs. The round yellow sign with the X and RR is an advance warning that stands seven hundred fifty feet before the track. The crossbuck is a different sign that stands at the crossing itself and may carry a sign below it showing how many tracks there are. If a question asks which sign is placed seven hundred fifty feet ahead, the answer is the round yellow one, not the crossbuck. Think of it as the round sign telling you a crossing is coming, and the crossbuck telling you that you have arrived. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Buses and hazardous-material trucks.
Stop within fifteen to fifty feet.

narration.text: Some vehicles must stop before every railroad crossing: school buses, church buses, all passenger buses, and trucks hauling flammables, explosives or other hazardous material. The manual says a stop at a railroad crossing must be made within fifteen to fifty feet of it. Approach slowly enough to be sure you can stop once a train first comes into view, and come to a complete stop at crossings protected by electric or mechanical signals as the manual directs. If you follow one of these buses or trucks, expect it to stop. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Buses and hazmat trucks: every crossing.
Others: lights, gates or a train.

narration.text: Here is a second trap. Buses and hazardous-material trucks must stop at every railroad crossing, whether or not a train is in sight. Other drivers must stop when there are flashing lights, lowered gates or an approaching train. So if a question describes an ordinary car at a quiet crossing with no warning active, the car is not required to make the same automatic stop as a bus, though it should still approach slowly and look and listen. And everyone must stop when the gate is down or a train is coming. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Which vehicles stop at every crossing?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: which vehicles must stop before every railroad crossing? Decide first, then compare. The answer is school buses, church buses, all passenger buses, and trucks hauling flammables, explosives or other hazardous material. These vehicles always stop, within fifteen to fifty feet of the crossing. Other drivers must stop for flashing lights, lowered gates or an approaching train. If you are driving behind one of these buses or trucks, be ready for its stop, so you are not surprised when it slows at the tracks. Trains cannot stop quickly, so the warnings are there to protect you.

lines.text: Round sign, markings, lights, gates, crossbuck.
Stop when warned; buses always.

narration.text: To finish, the round yellow sign stands seven hundred fifty feet before the track, the pavement may show an X with two R's, a yellow no-passing line and white stop lines, and the crossbuck marks the crossing and may show the number of tracks. Flashing lights always mean stop, and with gates you wait until they rise and the lights stop. With no device, slow, look and listen. Buses and hazardous-material trucks always stop, within fifteen to fifty feet. You must stop for a lowered gate or approaching train, and make sure every track is clear.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter gathers the railroad safety tips. The stakes are high. The manual reports that crossing crashes kill more people in the United States each year than all aviation crashes together, that Alabama ranks thirteenth nationally for highway-railroad crossing deaths, and that a crash with a train makes a motorist forty times more likely to die. You will learn the habits that prevent these crashes: how to handle gears on the tracks, expecting trains, watching for a second train, gates, following buses, staying off tracks, and what to do if you stall.

lines.text: Never change gears on the tracks.
Do not start across unless you can clear.

narration.text: Never change gears while you are on the tracks, because that can stall the car; if you drive a manual transmission, shift down before you cross. Expect a train on any track at any hour, day or night. In heavy traffic, do not start across the tracks until you know you can clear the crossing, so you are never trapped on the rails waiting for cars ahead to move. Walking or playing on tracks, trestles, rail yards or equipment is illegal, and you should cross tracks only at designated crossings. Always expect a train. A few seconds of patience can save your life.

lines.text: Never drive around lowered gates.
Never race a train.

narration.text: Driving around lowered gates is against the law, so stay put until they rise, and never race a train to the crossing. Even if you think you can make it, the risk is not worth it. Be ready to stop when you follow buses or trucks that are required to stop at crossings, because they will stop even when no train is visible. The manual also notes that nearly half of train-vehicle collisions happen at crossings with active warning devices, which shows how often drivers ignore or try to outrun the warnings in front of them. Always expect a train. A few seconds of patience can save your life.

lines.text: One train passing is not the end.
Check every track before crossing.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When the last car of a train passes, many drivers start across right away. But another train may be coming on a different track, sometimes from the opposite direction, and the first train can hide it from view. After the last car passes, wait until you are sure no second train is coming on another track. Expect a train on any track at any time. The few seconds you spend checking can be the difference between a safe crossing and a crash with a train that you never saw coming. Always expect a train. A few seconds of patience can save your life.

lines.text: Get everyone out and away.
A freight train needs a mile.

narration.text: If your vehicle stalls on a crossing, get everyone out right away and clear of the tracks, then call local law enforcement for help. Do not stay in the car trying to restart it. The reason is simple: trains cannot stop quickly. A freight train going fifty-five miles per hour needs a mile or more to stop, about the length of eighteen football fields. By the time the engineer sees your car, it is far too late for the train to stop. Your only safe move is to get everyone away from the tracks. Always expect a train. A few seconds of patience can save your life.

lines.text: After the last car passes, what?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: after the last car of a train passes, what should you check before crossing? Settle on your answer first. The answer is that no second train is coming on another track, especially from the opposite direction. A second train can follow on another track, and the first train may have blocked your view of it. Wait until you are sure every track is clear. And remember the other tips: never drive around lowered gates, never race a train, and never change gears while on the tracks. Always expect a train. A few seconds of patience can save your life.

Stalled? Everyone out.

narration.text: To close the chapter, do not change gears on the tracks, expect a train on any track at any hour, and do not start across unless you can clear it. After a train passes, watch for a second one. Never drive around lowered gates or race a train, and be ready to stop behind buses and trucks that must stop. Stay off tracks and trestles and cross only at designated crossings. If you stall, get everyone out and away, then call law enforcement, because a freight train needs a mile or more to stop. Crossing crashes are deadlier than all aviation crashes.
